introduction: A traveller meets a man weeping over his dying dog, with a bag of bread on his back: “I said I loved the dog, but not enough to share my bread with him.” The guide opens with stories of that kind, then looks for selfishness where it hides (in piety, in leadership, in “we only wish what you wish”), calls the insistent self by the name of Satan, and turns at last toward a life centred elsewhere and given to others’ good. The New Testament has the same parables and the same diagnosis: the rich fool, Lazarus at the gate, the chief seats, Diotrephes who loved preeminence, “lovers of their own selves”. The Qur’an speaks of the soul that commands evil and of desire taken for a god, and praises those who prefer others in their own poverty. Hillel’s saying and the commandment to love one’s neighbour “as thyself” keep a place for a right self-regard, as reading 9 does. Adam Smith and Whitman test the boundary from two sides: one shows self-interest feeding the town, the other a self so large it leaves no one out.
questions: “I loved the dog, but not enough to share my bread.” Why does the guide begin with a story and not a definition?
Adam Smith says we owe our dinner to the baker’s self-interest. Is the selfishness the readings condemn the same thing as the self-interest he describes?
“Love thy neighbour as thyself”; “if I am not for myself, who will be for me?” What kind of concern for oneself do reading 9 and these sayings approve?
Reading 7 says a person may be selfish in the extreme and not know it. By what means could one find out?
Whitman celebrates a self that contains everyone; reading 42 asks for renunciation of self. Can both lead to “the betterment of the lives of one another”?

outside.why: Fine sayings “are but words”, seldom carried into action. If one of you say, Be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?

A man loves his dying dog, but not enough to share his bread. Whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?
The rich man fared sumptuously every day, and the beggar at his gate desired to be fed with the crumbs.
A well is capped so that others may not drink. Isaiah on the worship God wants: is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?
People keep their possessions for their own enjoyment. I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and I will say to my soul, Soul, take thine ease. But God said unto him, Thou fool.

Adam Smith observed that it is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. A great deal of the world’s bread arrives by self-love. What does the reading’s “winter of selfishness” say to that?
Some love “for some ulterior purpose”; he expects reward from none. We feed you for the sake of God only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you.
Selfishness has “exceedingly subtle forms”, and a person may be ignorant of it. The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
The Sermon on the Mount hunts it in piety itself: they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast.

Mere selfish love is disastrous, but “spiritual and conscious devotion to self” can be a spur upward. The second great commandment takes love of self as its measure: thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. What is the self-love that the commandment assumes and the readings allow?
Hillel holds both halves in one saying: if I am not for myself, who will be for me? And when I am for myself alone, what am I? And if not now, when?
Love your country not because it is yours alone but as part of a larger whole. Asked where he came from, Diogenes said: I am a citizen of the world.
Self-love is “the means of the destruction of many important souls”. In the last days men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud.
What delays the Cause is “love for leadership and self-interest”. The elder writes of one such in an early church: Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.
They love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues, and to be called of men, Rabbi.
A position sought for personal interest injures the public. Whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister.
Parties “work for their own personal gains”. Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?
The peoples exert every effort for their own material interests. Ruskin’s reply to the economics of his century: there is no wealth but life.
Those who play for their own small ends “perish of their own futility”. No man is an island, entire of itself; any man’s death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind.

Those who chase pleasure imagine they enjoy life, and are scattered by it. Mill found the same in himself: ask yourself whether you are happy, and you cease to be so; those only are happy who have their minds fixed on some object other than their own happiness.
Despair is the harvest of self-indulgence. He that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption.
They take the rivulet of their self-love for a sea of universal sympathy. The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself: God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are.
“What is Satan?” “The insistent self.” Joseph in the Qur’an: I do not exculpate myself. Lo! the human soul enjoineth unto evil, save that whereon my Lord hath mercy.
The self’s rulership is bondage. To be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.
Those who worship their own desires outnumber the rest. The Qur’an: hast thou seen him who maketh his desire his god?
“Deliver your souls … from the bondage of self.” Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free.
No peace save by renouncing thyself. If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.

Whitman begins his great poem: I celebrate myself, and sing myself; and what I assume you shall assume, for every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you. His self is not renounced but enlarged until it includes everyone. Is that a rival to the reading’s way, or the same road from the other end?
Centre your thoughts in the Well-Beloved rather than in yourselves. I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.
One person thinks always of himself, another of Truth. Charity seeketh not her own.
Believers should not be occupied with themselves. We that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
That they “give preference to others”. The Qur’an praises the people of Medina who received the emigrants: they prefer the fugitives above themselves though poverty become their lot.
The Prophet’s test of faith: none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
The slightest alloy of self-interest makes every effort fruitless. Though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.
Men should strive for the betterment of one another’s lives. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.
Paul’s shortest form of it: let no man seek his own, but every man another’s wealth.

shortfall: Some readings are comments on particular persons and parties, or single sentences that repeat the warning against following self and desire; they share the companions of their neighbours.
